A weekday sourdough that fits around work

Posted on 2 November 2025 by Ruth

Sourdough is less a recipe than a relationship. The starter in the jar on my counter is eleven years old, and in that time it has survived two house moves, a fortnight in a cool box at a campsite, and one memorable week when my neighbour fed it with rye flour instead of white.

What follows is the method I actually use on a weekday, not the one in the glossy books. It fits around a working day, it needs no special equipment beyond a lidded pot, and it forgives most of the mistakes I made in my first year.

The night before

Start the evening before. Take a tablespoon of starter, add fifty grams of flour and fifty grams of water, stir, cover and leave it on the counter. By morning it should have doubled and smell sharp and a little like yoghurt. If it has not risen, your kitchen is cold: put the jar in the oven with only the light on.

Mixing

In the morning, mix 450 grams of strong white flour, 50 grams of wholemeal and 350 grams of water until no dry flour remains. Leave it for an hour. This rest, the autolyse, lets the flour hydrate and does half of the kneading for you.

Add 100 grams of the levain and 10 grams of salt, then squeeze the dough through your fingers until everything is evenly mixed. It will feel wet and ragged. That is fine; resist the urge to add more flour.

Over the next three hours, give the dough four sets of stretches and folds, one every thirty to forty minutes. Wet your hand, lift one side of the dough, stretch it up until it resists, and fold it over the rest. Turn the bowl a quarter and repeat four times. Each set takes under a minute.

After the last fold, leave the dough alone until it has grown by about half, has a domed, bubbly surface, and jiggles when you shake the bowl. Depending on the temperature this takes anywhere from two to six hours. This bulk fermentation is where most loaves succeed or fail, and the clock is a poor guide: watch the dough.

Shaping and the overnight rest

Tip the dough onto an unfloured counter and shape it into a tight round by dragging it towards you with a bench scraper. Let it rest for twenty minutes, then shape it again, more tightly, and place it seam side up in a floured bowl or basket.

Cover the basket and put it in the fridge overnight. The cold retard slows the yeast while the bacteria keep working, which is where the flavour comes from. It also means you bake at a time that suits you rather than the dough.

Baking

To bake, put a lidded cast-iron pot in the oven and heat it to 250 degrees for forty-five minutes. Turn the cold dough out onto a sheet of baking paper, slash it once along its length with a razor blade, and lower it into the pot. Bake with the lid on for twenty minutes, then with the lid off at 230 degrees for another twenty to twenty-five, until the crust is deeply browned.

Let it cool for at least an hour before you cut it. I know. But the crumb is still setting as it cools, and a loaf cut hot is gummy in a way that has nothing to do with your baking.

If the loaf spreads flat, the bulk fermentation went too long or the shaping was too loose. If it is dense with a few large holes near the top, it went too short. Change one thing at a time, write it down, and within a month you will know your starter and your kitchen better than any recipe can.
